issue: Formal boilerplate slightly wrong: real surat keterangan certificates close with 'untuk dipergunakan sebagaimana mestinya' (or digunakan) — 'dipakai' is too casual for this fixed formula, and the whole point of the card is the authentic wording.

fix.target: Surat keterangan kerja ini dibuat untuk dipergunakan sebagaimana mestinya.
fix.english: This employment certificate is issued to be used as appropriate.

newTokens.dipergunakan: be used (formal certificate boilerplate, from guna)

issue: Formal sign card lacks a register-naming tip: the tip is pure morphology (peN-) and never tells the learner this is sign language or what people actually say. Policy rule 4 requires formal cards to name the register.

fix.target: Area ini khusus untuk pemegang kartu anggota.
fix.english: This area is exclusively for membership card holders.
fix.grammar: Sign word: pemegang kartu = 'card holder' (peN- = the holder) — spoken: yang punya kartu anggota.

issue: Inaccurate everyday-equivalent in tip: 'speech often servis' is misleading here — servis means repair/maintenance service (servis motor); for layanan pelanggan people say CS, never 'servis pelanggan'. The tip risks teaching a wrong collocation.

fix.target: Layanan pelanggan kami dapat dihubungi dua puluh empat jam.
fix.english: Our customer service can be reached twenty-four hours a day.
fix.grammar: layanan = formal 'service', from melayani — in speech, customer service is just CS (ce-es).

issue: The formal Indonesian is off: bank notices say 'penarikan (tunai)' for withdrawals and ask customers to 'konfirmasi/dikonfirmasi sehari sebelumnya' — 'pengambilan uang ... harap dilaporkan' (be reported) is not how any bank phrases it. Tip repeats the wrong noun.

fix.target: Penarikan uang di atas sepuluh juta harap dikonfirmasi sehari sebelumnya.
fix.english: Withdrawals above ten million should be confirmed one day in advance.
fix.grammar: penarikan uang = 'withdrawal', bank language — spoken: mau ambil uang.

issue: Gloss overtranslates: pahit banget = 'really bitter', not 'way too bitter' — 'too' would be terlalu/kepahitan. The card teaches banget = sekali/sangat, so the gloss should not smuggle in excess.

fix.target: Kopi di kedai baru itu pahit banget menurutku.
fix.english: The coffee at that new cafe is really bitter, if you ask me.

issue: Internal register clash: 'akhir pekan' is flagged by this deck's own tip (id-3132) as the news word — 'in conversation everyone says weekend or Sabtu-Minggu' — yet here it sits in a slang card next to 'lagi ngapain'. Recast with the conversational form.

fix.target: Dia tanya aku lagi ngapain Sabtu-Minggu ini.
fix.english: She asked what I was up to this weekend.

issue: Incoherent register mix: nobody who softens with dong asks 'seru tidak?' — the natural tag with dong is 'seru nggak?'. nggak is already sanctioned in this node (id-3176ff), so the fix stays within taught material.

fix.target: Cerita dong, liburanmu di Bali kemarin seru nggak?
fix.english: Come on, tell me — was your Bali trip fun or not?

issue: Colloquial card missing its register tip: this is the first (and only) occurrence of the interjection 'duh' in the slice and the card has no grammar tip at all — policy rule 3 requires sanctioned colloquials to carry a tip.

fix.target: Duh, aku ketinggalan dompet di rumah lagi.
fix.english: Ugh, I left my wallet at home again.
fix.grammar: Duh = 'ugh/oh no', the spoken groan for small disasters: duh, ketinggalan dompet!

issue: Internal register clash: the deck's own tip (id-3112) says 'in real life everyone says HP', yet this everyday-speech card (a parent nagging a child) uses written-register 'ponsel'. In node-36 the spoken word belongs in the sentence.

fix.target: Jangan main HP terus, matamu bisa sakit.
fix.english: Stop playing on your phone all the time — your eyes will hurt.
fix.grammar: Main HP = 'be on your phone' — HP (ha-pe) is what everyone calls a phone in speech.
